chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter starts from a carpenter's problem: how must two wooden strips be joined so that a thread through their ends makes a rectangle? Answering it needs deductions, and each later family (square, parallelogram, rhombus, kite, trapezium) is met the same way: define it, predict a property, prove it with congruent triangles or parallel lines, then check it by constructing and measuring.

points.title: Predict, then prove
points.text: Every concept opens with a question the student answers first, such as whether the diagonals of a parallelogram are equal, and then a short deduction settles it.

points.title: Measuring makes a conjecture, reasoning makes it sure
points.text: Constructions and measurements suggest a property; only a deduction shows it holds for every quadrilateral of that kind.

points.title: One shape, several names
points.text: A square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rhombus is a parallelogram and a kite. Venn diagrams make the family visible.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: crossing strips, dragging a quadrilateral, a square in a square, tearing and placing the four angles, sides and angles, a hinged rhombus, diagonals, sliding kites and trapeziums, and sorting figures into the family rings.

concepts.concept_name: What makes a figure a quadrilateral?

content.text:
In this chapter, we will study some interesting types of four-sided figures and solve problems based on them. Such figures are commonly known as quadrilaterals. The word 'quadrilateral' is derived from Latin words, quadri meaning four, and latus referring to sides.
Observe the following figures.
Figs. (i), (ii), and (iii) are quadrilaterals, and the others are not. Why?
The angles of a quadrilateral are the angles between its sides, as marked in Figs. (i), (ii), and (iii).
We will start with the most familiar quadrilaterals, rectangles and squares.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a carpenter's workshop is full of frames. Which of them are quadrilaterals, and which are not?
2. A quadrilateral is a closed figure made of exactly four straight sides that meet only at their ends.
3. A figure with a curved side, an open gap, or more than four sides is not a quadrilateral.
4. The angles of a quadrilateral are the four angles between its sides, one at each corner.
5. Keep this question open: the carpenter wants a frame that is exactly rectangular. How can she be sure it is?

concepts.concept_name: The Carpenter's Problem: the other strip

content.text:
4.1 Rectangles and Squares
Rectangle: A rectangle is a quadrilateral in which (i) The angles are all right angles (90°), and (ii) The opposite sides are of equal length.
Are there other ways to define a rectangle?
A carpenter needs to put together two thin strips of wood so that when a thread is passed through their endpoints, it forms a rectangle. She already has one 8 cm long strip. What should be the length of the other strip? Where should they both be joined?
1. What is the length of the other diagonal? 2. What is the point of intersection of the two diagonals? 3. What should the angle be between the diagonals?
Since ABCD is a rectangle, we have AB = CD, ∠BAD = ∠CDA = 90°, and AD is common to both triangles. So, ∆ADC ≅ ∆DAB by the SAS congruence condition.
Therefore, AC = BD. This shows that the diagonals of a rectangle always have the same length.

concepts.concept_name: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other

content.text:
Deduction 2: What is the point of intersection of the two diagonals?
The blue angles are equal since they are vertically opposite angles. In order to show congruence, consider ∠1 and ∠2. Are they equal?
Since ∠B is a right angle, ∠1 and ∠3 together make a right angle. In ∆BCD, ∠3 and ∠2 together also make a right angle, because ∠C is a right angle. So, ∠1 = ∠2, each being 90° minus ∠3.
Thus, by the AAS condition for congruence, ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD. Hence OA = OC and OB = OD.
When the diagonals cross at their midpoints, we say that the diagonals bisect each other. Bisecting a quantity means dividing it into two equal parts.
Can the following equalities be used to establish that ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB? AO = CO (proved above), ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite angles), AD = CB.

content.text:
Worked example: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and AC = 8 cm. Find OA, OC, OB and OD.
1. In ∆AOB and ∆COD: AB = CD, ∠AOB = ∠COD (vertically opposite), and ∠ABD = ∠CDB (each is 90° minus the same angle).
2. By the AAS condition, ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD, so OA = OC and OB = OD.
3. The diagonals are equal, so BD = AC = 8 cm.
4. Each half is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 cm.
Answer: OA = OC = OB = OD = 4 cm; the strips are joined at their midpoints

concepts.concept_name: Equal diagonals that bisect each other make a rectangle

content.text:
Deduction 3: What are the angles between the diagonals?
Let us check what quadrilateral we get if we draw the two diagonals such that their lengths are equal, they bisect each other and have an arbitrary angle, say 60°, between them. Can you find all the remaining angles?
In ∆AOB, since OA = OB, the angles opposite them are equal, say a. a + a + 60 = 180. Therefore 2a = 120. Thus a = 60.
We can see that ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB. Hence, AB = CD, and AD = CB. Therefore, ABCD is a rectangle.
Carpenters in Europe use this method to get a rectangular frame. Farmers in Mozambique, a country in Africa, use this method while constructing houses to get the base of the house in a rectangular shape.
The Process of Finding Properties: observations through measurement give useful insights, but with them we can only form a conjecture, a statement about which we are highly confident, but not yet sure if it always holds true. The only way we can be sure is by justifying or proving the statement.
Note to the Teacher: Gently encourage students to deduce or justify properties. Whenever students face challenges, encourage them to experiment and observe, and use their intuition.

In ∆AOB, since OA = OB, the angles opposite them are equal, say a. a + a + 60 = 180. Therefore 2a = 120. Thus a = 60.
We can see that ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB. Hence, AB = CD, and AD = CB. Therefore, ABCD is a rectangle.

Carpenters in Europe use this method to get a rectangular frame. Farmers in Mozambique, a country in Africa, use this method while constructing houses to get the base of the house in a rectangular shape.

The Process of Finding Properties: observations through measurement give useful insights, but with them we can only form a conjecture, a statement about which we are highly confident, but not yet sure if it always holds true. The only way we can be sure is by justifying or proving the statement.
Note to the Teacher: Gently encourage students to deduce or justify properties. Whenever students face challenges, encourage them to experiment and observe, and use their intuition.

content.text:
1. Predict first: two equal strips cross at their midpoints at 60°. Will the thread make a rectangle, or some slanted shape?
2. The angles at O are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°, by vertically opposite angles and linear pairs.
3. All four half-diagonals are equal, so each small triangle is isosceles: the 60° triangles have base angles 60°, the 120° triangles have base angles 30°.
4. Every corner is 60° + 30° = 90°, and congruent triangles give equal opposite sides: a rectangle.
5. Carpenters in Europe and farmers in Mozambique use exactly this to set out rectangles.
6. Measuring many rectangles only gives a conjecture; this deduction is what makes us sure.

content.text:
Worked example: Two equal diagonals bisect each other and meet at 60°. Find all the angles of the quadrilateral ABCD and say what it is.
1. The four angles at O are 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°.
2. In ∆AOB, OA = OB, so its two base angles are equal. Their sum is 180 − 60 = 120, so each is 120 ÷ 2 = 60.
3. In ∆AOD the angle at O is 120°, so its base angles add to 180 − 120 = 60, and each is 30.
4. Each corner of ABCD is made of one angle of each kind: 60 + 30 = 90.
5. ∆AOB ≅ ∆COD and ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB by SAS, so AB = CD and AD = CB.
Answer: Every angle of ABCD is 90° and its opposite sides are equal, so ABCD is a rectangle

content.text:
Take one of the angles between the diagonals as x. We can compute the four angles between the diagonals to be x, x, 180 − x, and 180 − x.
a = (180 − x)/2 = 90 − x/2. Similarly, in the isosceles ∆AOD, let the base angles be b. b = x/2.
All the angles of the quadrilateral are a + b, which is 90 − x/2 + x/2 = 90.
Hence, no matter what the angles between the diagonals are, if the diagonals are equal and they bisect each other, the quadrilateral is a rectangle.

Worked example: Equal diagonals bisect each other at 40°. Find the angles of the quadrilateral.
1. In the triangle with 40° at O, the base angles add to 180 − 40 = 140, so each is 140 ÷ 2 = 70.
2. The next triangle has 180 − 40 = 140 at O, so its base angles add to 180 − 140 = 40, and each is 20.
3. Each corner of the quadrilateral is 70 + 20 = 90.
Answer: All four angles are 90°, so it is again a rectangle

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 2): Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm that bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of (i) 30° (ii) 40° (iii) 90° (iv) 140°.
1. Draw AC = 8 cm and mark its midpoint O, so OA = OC = 4 cm.
2. At O draw a line making the given angle with OC.
3. On this line mark B and D on opposite sides of O with OB = OD = 4 cm, so BD = 8 cm.
4. Join A, B, C and D in order.
5. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so each figure is a rectangle; at 90° all four sides are also equal.
Answer: All four are rectangles; the one with diagonals at 90° is a square

content.text:
Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 4): We have seen how to get 90° using paper folding. Now, suppose we do not have any paper but two sticks of equal length, and a thread. How do we make an exact 90° using these?
1. Cross the two equal sticks so that their midpoints meet at O.
2. Pass the thread round the four ends of the sticks in order.
3. The sticks are equal diagonals that bisect each other, so the thread makes a rectangle.
4. Every corner of a rectangle is 90°, so the thread turns through an exact 90° at each stick end.
Answer: Cross the sticks at their midpoints and run the thread round the four ends; each corner of the thread is exactly 90°

content.text:
Worked example: ABCD has all four angles 90°. Show that AD = CB and DC = BA, and say why writing ∆BAD ≅ ∆CDB is wrong.
1. Join the diagonal BD.
2. ∠BAD = ∠DCB = 90°, and BD is common to ∆BAD and ∆DCB.
3. ∠ABD + ∠DBC = 90° and ∠CDB + ∠DBC = 90°, so ∠ABD = ∠CDB.
4. By AAS, ∆BAD ≅ ∆DCB, matching B with D, A with C and D with B.
5. So AD = CB and BA = DC.
6. ∆CDB would match A with D, but the right angle at A matches the right angle at C, not D.
Answer: AD = CB and DC = BA; ∆BAD ≅ ∆CDB is wrong because the vertices are not in matching order

concepts.concept_name: Opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel

content.text:
Property 1: All the angles of a rectangle are 90°.
Property 2: The opposite sides of a rectangle are equal.
Are the opposite sides of a rectangle parallel? AB acts as a transversal to AD and BC, and ∠A + ∠B = 90° + 90° = 180°. When the sum of the internal angles on the same side of the transversal is 180°, the lines are parallel. So AD || BC.
Can you similarly show that AB is parallel to DC (AB||DC)?
Property 3: The opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel to each other.
Property 4: The diagonals of a rectangle are of equal length and they bisect each other.

content.text:
1. Predict first: are the opposite sides of a rectangle parallel, and how could you be sure without measuring?
2. Take a side as a transversal: the two angles on the same side of it are 90° and 90°, adding to 180°.
3. Internal angles on the same side adding to 180° means the lines are parallel.
4. So a rectangle has all angles 90°, opposite sides equal, opposite sides parallel, and equal diagonals that bisect each other.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch. 4 Quadrilaterals (formerly NCERT Ch. 3 Understanding Quadrilaterals), sections on the parallelogram and its special cases. This is the chapter opener and it runs BEFORE any family is named or any property is proved, so nothing here is justified by a criterion the class has not met: the families are held BY CONSTRUCTION and the tool only reports what the construction does and does not fix. The hierarchy is inclusive, as the chapter states it: the rectangle keeps all four of the parallelogram's statements and adds two, which the tool shows as the count 0 subset 4 subset 6.

overview.goal: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A light coordinate grid on a plain working ground, the way a shape is pinned out on squared paper with its corners still free to move. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class looks at one drawn parallelogram, calls it a rectangle because it looks like one, and the figure itself is asked to settle whether those right angles were ever really there.
overview.concept: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
overview.purpose: The student distinguishes a property that always holds from one that only holds for the drawn case, and says why the surviving property cannot be broken.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Figure fills the main panel with the readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into an expandable strip beneath on a 390 px frame. The property panel sits under the readouts. No two vertex handles are ever drawn closer than 60 px. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the property panel while a prediction is still open, and never render a self crossing or flattened figure. A degenerate figure would give the readouts nothing honest to say.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

media.description: A quadrilateral stands on squared paper with four draggable corners, its equal sides marked with matching hatch strokes, its equal angles with matching arcs and every right angle with the small square the textbook uses. Beside it eight statements each carry a live tick that lights only while the statement holds at the position on screen, and a badge that says whether the CONSTRUCTION keeps it. Dragging is what separates the two: the four statements a parallelogram is built to satisfy never go out however the figure is pulled about, while equal diagonals and four right angles light up in the one position where the parallelogram happens to look like a rectangle and are struck through the moment the next drag lands, labelled with the position number that broke them. The same eight statements are then put to a free quadrilateral, where not one of them survives, so the kept list reads as a fact about how a figure was built rather than about how it currently looks. Side lengths, angles, both diagonal lengths and the two halves at O are all derived from one measure function on the stored vertex coordinates, so no two numbers on the screen can disagree, and near collinear, self crossing, zero length and off paper positions are refused before the drag completes with the reason drawn at the corner that caused it.

concept.notation: Equal sides are marked with matching ticks and equal angles with matching arcs. A property that survives every drag is written in the kept list, one that does not is left out.
concept.statement: A figure drawn once can look as though it has properties it does not have. Dragging separates the two: a property forced by the construction survives every legal position, while a property that happened to hold in the drawn case switches off as soon as the figure moves. What survives dragging is what the family really guarantees.
prerequisites: the names of the special quadrilaterals
misconceptions: A property judged from a single drawn case, so a parallelogram that happens to look like a rectangle is credited with right angles.
Prototypical images, where a figure is recognised only in its standard orientation and not when it is turned.
concept.why_it_is_true: The construction fixes some relations and leaves the rest free. A relation that the construction fixes cannot fail, because every legal position was built to satisfy it. A relation that the construction leaves free will fail somewhere, and dragging is a search for that somewhere. Failing to break a constructed property is therefore evidence of a very different kind from measuring one figure.
worked_numbers: In a constructed parallelogram the opposite sides stay equal through every drag, and the readouts move together.
In the same parallelogram the diagonals are equal only in the positions where it happens to be a rectangle, and one drag switches that tick off.
In a free quadrilateral even the opposite sides stop being equal, so almost nothing is kept.

answer_key.worked: A property that survives every legal drag is guaranteed by the family; one that switches off under dragging was only true of the drawn case.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn figure: which listed properties hold at the current vertices, and which of them are forced by the family rather than incidental.
answer_key.precision: All measures are derived from the stored vertex coordinates. Equality is judged with a tolerance of 0.5 degrees and 0.01 units, and the tolerance is stated in the feedback rather than hidden.
answer_key.ground_truth: measures(vertices) = the four side lengths, four angles and two diagonal lengths, computed from the points. holds(property, measures) = the predicate evaluated at the current position. alwaysHolds(family, property) = the family's true property set, held as data and never inferred from the drawn case.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the difference between the two badges visible before any drag has happened. Four statements read Kept and four read Not true now, on ONE figure, and the class can already see that the panel is answering two different questions: is it true here, and can it ever fail.

Beat 2 is the whole argument in one motion. The figure walks three positions; at the middle one the diagonals land on the same number and all four angles land on 90, so two extra ticks light. The next position turns both of them off and the tool strikes them through with the position number that broke them, while the four Kept ticks never so much as flicker. Say that every length on screen changed and the four Kept rows did not.

Beat 3 puts the identical eight statements to a figure built from four independent points. Not one tick is lit and the kept list holds 0. That is the point to name: the panel is a report about the CONSTRUCTION, not a description of the picture.

Figure it Out (rectangles and squares, question 5): We saw that one of the properties of a rectangle is that its opposite sides are parallel. Can this be chosen as a definition of a rectangle? In other words, is every quadrilateral that has opposite sides parallel and equal, a rectangle?
1. Draw two pairs of parallel lines that do not meet at right angles.
2. They make a quadrilateral with opposite sides parallel and equal, for example with angles 60°, 120°, 60° and 120°.
3. Its angles are not 90°, so it is not a rectangle.
Answer: No; a slanted parallelogram has opposite sides parallel and equal but is not a rectangle

Figure it Out (kites and trapeziums, question 5): If PAIR and RODS are two rectangles, find ∠IOD. (O lies on AI, ∠ORI = 30°, PR = 5 cm and RS = 5 cm.)
1. In ∆ROI, ∠RIO = 90° because PAIR is a rectangle, and ∠ORI = 30°.
